title: Locking: from locks to correct schedules
lead: A lock controls access to a data object. A locking protocol specifies when a transaction may acquire and release its locks.
goals: Simulate shared/exclusive locks and the two locking phases
Handle deadlocks through detection or timestamp-based prevention

sections.title: The essential rules
sections.html:
Two people viewing an order can read it concurrently. When one updates the order, other transactions must be prevented from reading or writing the data protected by that update lock. Locks provide this access control.

An S-lock, or shared lock, permits reading. Multiple transactions may hold S-locks on the same object. An X-lock, or exclusive lock, permits writing and conflicts with other transactions' S-locks and X-locks.

Two-phase locking (2PL) has two phases. In the growing phase, a transaction may acquire or upgrade locks. An upgrade changes an S-lock to an X-lock when a reader needs to write; it must wait until other holders’ incompatible locks are gone. The transaction’s first lock release begins the shrinking phase, during which it may only release locks. It therefore cannot acquire or upgrade a lock after releasing one.

In this lecture, strict 2PL retains all locks until the transaction ends. Some sources call retention of both S-locks and X-locks rigorous 2PL, so state the convention you are using.

Key takeaway

The first lock release is the phase boundary in 2PL. A transaction cannot return to acquiring locks afterward. The lecture's strict variant additionally delays every release until transaction completion.

Online locking and the phase boundary

A lock manager keeps holders and waiting requests. S/S is compatible; an X lock permits its holder to read and write, while excluding other transactions' S and X locks. Locks must protect every relevant access, and lock modes alone do not make an arbitrary acquire/release pattern serializable.

Original unsafe sequence: T1 acquires X(A), writes A and releases X(A); T2 acquires X(A), writes A and releases it; T1 then acquires S(A) and reads A. The conflicting operations give T1→T2 and T2→T1. Every individual access was locked, but T1 acquired a lock after releasing one, violating 2PL.

Basic 2PL permits lock release before commit once the growing phase ends. Another transaction can then read an uncommitted value; if its writer aborts, that reader may also have to abort. Retaining locks until completion prevents this cascading-abort risk under the lecture's strict convention.

Does holding an appropriate lock for every individual access alone guarantee 2PL?

Worked answer. No. A transaction must also obey the growing/shrinking rule. The example locks each access but acquires S(A) after an unlock.

Does an appropriate lock for each individual access prove that 2PL was followed?

Worked answer. No. Acquisition and upgrade requests must also obey the phase boundary. Acquiring S(A) after an earlier unlock violates 2PL even if that particular read is locked.

sections.title: Worked example: updating an order
sections.html:
T1 needs to update Order and Stock. The sequence X(Order), update Order, unlock(Order), X(Stock) violates 2PL at its final request. Replacing it with X(Order), X(Stock), update both, commit, unlock satisfies the lecture's strict variant.

T2, which only reads Order, must wait while T1 holds X(Order). If T1 aborts, T2 has never read the uncommitted version, so T2's result need not be withdrawn. This operational benefit goes beyond merely proving that a precedence graph is acyclic.

Trace the cascading-abort risk with an early unlock

Under basic 2PL, T1 can write Order and release its X-lock before committing, provided it acquires no further locks. T2 then reads that uncommitted value and uses it to update another object. If T1 aborts, T2 must also abort because its calculation depended on T1’s removed work. A third transaction that read T2’s uncommitted result would face the same problem. Under the lecture’s strict 2PL convention, T1 retains its lock until completion, so T2 cannot make the first dirty read.

How does retaining X(Order) until completion stop the cascading-abort chain?

Worked answer. It prevents T2 from acquiring an incompatible S(Order) and reading the uncommitted update. After T1 completes, T2 reads committed or restored data, so that first dirty dependency never forms.

sections.title: Deadlock and conflict cycles
sections.html:
Suppose T1 holds X(Order) and T2 holds X(Stock). T1 requests Stock, while T2 requests Order. The waits-for graph contains T1 → T2 → T1. T1 cannot proceed until T2 releases Stock, and T2 cannot proceed until T1 releases Order.

Key takeaway

Waits-for graphs and precedence graphs answer different questions. A waits-for graph records who is waiting for whom to detect deadlock. A precedence graph records the order of conflicting operations to check conflict serializability.

Aborting T2, undoing its changes, and releasing Stock lets T1 proceed. Victim selection should consider work already performed and previous restarts to avoid starvation. Preclaiming all required locks as one all-or-nothing request at the start avoids holding some locks while waiting for others, but it requires knowing the lock set in advance. Merely requesting locks one by one at the start does not provide this guarantee.

Removing a deadlock, or preventing one

A waits-for edge points from a blocked transaction to a transaction holding its requested lock. Deadlock detection finds a cycle and chooses a victim; the choice can consider rollback cost, work already performed and starvation. Conservative locking avoids hold-and-wait only when the entire known lock set is granted atomically, not when requests are merely issued one at a time at the start.

The next section chooses who may wait using transaction ages. That prevents cycles by controlling every newly created waiting edge.

Why is requesting all needed locks sequentially different from granting them atomically?

Worked answer. Sequential requests can leave a transaction holding one lock while waiting for another, allowing a cycle. Atomic all-or-nothing preclaiming removes that hold-and-wait pattern.

Why are sequential requests for all locks different from atomic preclaiming?

Worked answer. Sequential requests can leave a transaction holding an already granted lock while waiting for another. Atomic all-or-nothing granting avoids that intermediate hold-and-wait state; knowing the lock list alone is insufficient.

sections.title: Reasoning with timestamps
sections.html:
T_old has timestamp 10 and T_new has timestamp 30. A smaller timestamp means that the transaction started earlier.

  • Wait-die: if old requests a lock held by new, old waits; if new requests a lock held by old, new aborts.
  • Wound-wait: if old requests a lock held by new, new is forced to abort; if new requests a lock held by old, new waits.

Why these rules prevent a waiting cycle

With smaller timestamps meaning older transactions, wait-die permits an older requester to wait for a younger holder. Every waiting edge therefore has an increasing timestamp. Wound-wait permits a younger requester to wait for an older holder, so every waiting edge has a decreasing timestamp. A strictly monotone chain cannot return to its start. A restarted transaction retains its original timestamp to avoid repeatedly becoming the youngest.

T_new requests a lock held by T_old. Who waits under each rule?

Worked answer. In wait-die, the younger requester T_new aborts. In wound-wait, T_new waits for the older holder. The waiting edge then goes from timestamp 30 to timestamp 10; it decreases, like every wound-wait waiting edge.

Timestamp 30 requests a lock held by timestamp 10. What happens?

Worked answer. Wait-die aborts the younger requester. Wound-wait lets it wait for the older holder, producing the decreasing edge 30→10. All permitted wound-wait waiting edges decrease, so they cannot form a cycle.

sections.title: Check your understanding
sections.html:
T1 acquires S(A), acquires S(B), releases S(A), and then upgrades S(B) to X(B). Is this valid? No. An upgrade after the shrinking phase has begun also violates 2PL.

Next question: does strict 2PL eliminate deadlock? No. Construct a counterexample with two transactions acquiring A and B in opposite orders. Serializability is a safety property; avoiding indefinite waits is a separate progress requirement.

Can a lock be upgraded after the first release, and does strict 2PL remove deadlocks?

Worked answer. The upgrade violates 2PL because shrinking has begun. Strict 2PL can still deadlock when transactions acquire A and B in opposite orders; detection or prevention addresses the waiting cycle.

quiz.question: T_old requests a lock held by T_new. What does wound-wait do?
options: T_new aborts and releases its locks
quiz.explanation: Under wound-wait, a transaction with a smaller timestamp can force a younger transaction holding the requested lock to abort.
